ip-addressing-and-subnets.r: Two teams each built a network using 10.0.0.0/16 and later needed to connect them. Peering was impossible because the ranges overlapped, and the only fix was to rebuild one network. A shared address plan made on day one would have cost an afternoon.
ip-addressing-and-subnets.x: Address space is a long-lived decision. Plan for growth, reserve ranges per environment and region, avoid overlap with offices and partners, and document it somewhere everyone reads. Ask what you will connect to in three years.

dns.r: A team moved a service to a new address and lowered nothing beforehand, so some users kept hitting the old server for hours because of a long record lifetime. Lowering the TTL a day before the change and raising it after became their standard step.
dns.x: DNS is a global cache you cannot flush. Plan changes around TTLs, keep records in code, monitor resolution from outside your network and remember that many outages are really DNS: expired domains, broken delegation or a single resolver.

http-and-tls.r: A site suddenly showed certificate warnings to every visitor. The certificate had expired because renewal depended on a calendar reminder. Automatic renewal with monitoring on days left removed the single point of human memory.
http-and-tls.x: Automate certificate issue and renewal, alert well before expiry, and know where each certificate is used. Understand the chain, SNI, protocol versions and what mutual TLS adds, and test failure modes, not just the happy path.

routing-and-nat.r: A new subnet could reach the internet but not an internal database. The route table had a default route but no route for the database network, so traffic went the wrong way. Reading the table from the host outward found it in minutes.
routing-and-nat.x: Most routing problems are asymmetry or a missing return path. Draw the packet path in both directions, remember that NAT hides sources and hurts debugging, and watch for overlapping routes and the longest-prefix rule.

troubleshooting-toolkit.r: A service reported it could not reach another. 'Connection refused' meant the host was reachable but nothing listened on the port, while 'timed out' would have pointed at a firewall or route. Reading the exact error saved the team from checking the wrong layer.
troubleshooting-toolkit.x: Debug in order and let each error narrow the search. Capture evidence from both ends, change one variable at a time, and write the result down. A repeatable sequence beats expertise when you are tired.

firewalls-and-load-balancing.r: A load balancer marked every server unhealthy after a deploy even though the app was fine. The health check path had been changed and now returned a redirect, which counted as failure. Aligning the check with a real health endpoint brought the servers back.
firewalls-and-load-balancing.x: Health checks decide who gets traffic, so make them cheap, honest and independent of heavy dependencies. Design for failure of a whole zone, set sensible timeouts and connection draining, and keep firewall rules minimal and reviewed.

vpn-and-tunnels.r: A site-to-site tunnel dropped every few hours and nobody knew why. Logs showed the two ends had different lifetime settings, so renegotiation failed. Matching the settings and adding monitoring on the tunnel state stopped the outages.
vpn-and-tunnels.x: Tunnels add failure modes: MTU, rekeying, asymmetric routes and a single gateway as a bottleneck. Run two tunnels, monitor them, keep keys rotated and decide what traffic really needs a VPN versus private connectivity.

ipv6-essentials.r: A service worked for most users but failed for a few on mobile networks. Their devices preferred IPv6, and the service had an AAAA record that pointed at a server that did not listen on IPv6. Either serving IPv6 properly or removing the record fixed it.
ipv6-essentials.x: Dual stack doubles your testing surface. Check that every layer handles both families, firewalls apply equally to IPv6 and monitoring covers it. Do not assume IPv4 rules protect IPv6 traffic.

latency-mtu-and-network-performance.r: Large file uploads stalled through a VPN while small requests worked. The path had a smaller MTU than the hosts assumed, and the messages that should have told the sender were blocked. Lowering the MTU on the tunnel made large transfers work.
latency-mtu-and-network-performance.x: Separate latency, bandwidth, loss and window sizes before tuning anything. Measure from the same vantage point as your users, test with realistic payloads and remember that retries can multiply load during trouble.

network-segmentation-and-security-groups.r: After a web server was compromised, the attacker could reach the database directly because the whole network was one flat zone. Splitting web, app and data tiers and allowing only the needed ports later limited what a single break-in could touch.
network-segmentation-and-security-groups.x: Segmentation limits blast radius only if rules stay tight. Prefer references between groups over address ranges, review rules regularly, log denied traffic and test that a compromised workload cannot move sideways.

dhcp-arp-and-the-local-network.r: Several machines lost connectivity at once after a switch change. Two devices had the same address, so neighbours kept updating their ARP tables to the wrong one. Tracking the duplicate through the ARP cache showed which device to fix.
dhcp-arp-and-the-local-network.x: Local-network failures look like random application errors. Know how leases, duplicates, VLAN tagging and ARP caches behave, monitor address pool exhaustion and keep static assignments documented.

debugging-network-problems.r: A request failed only from one office. Working up from link to DNS to routing to ports to TLS, the team found that the office resolver returned a stale record for a moved service. Flushing and fixing the resolver took ten minutes once the layer was known.
debugging-network-problems.x: Compare a working path with a broken one and find the first point where they differ. Keep packet captures for the hard cases, and remember the answer may be in a middlebox you do not own.

dns-tls-pki-dns-records-resolution-and-c.r: A team moved a website to a new load balancer and changed the record, but half the customers still reached the old address most of the day. The TTL was 86400 seconds. Next time they lowered it a day ahead and checked several resolvers.
dns-tls-pki-dns-records-resolution-and-c.x: TTL sets how fast a change spreads, so lower it before a planned move and test through more than one resolver. Treat DNS as a distributed cache, not a database you can update instantly.

dns-tls-pki-debugging-dns-failures.r: After a platform upgrade pod API calls slowed and DNS query volume grew tenfold. An added search domain plus ndots:5 made every external name try four suffixes first, and one suffix hit a slow forwarder. Fully qualified names and a node-local cache restored speed.
dns-tls-pki-debugging-dns-failures.x: Test from the same network position as the failing client. Private zones, split-horizon answers and Kubernetes search lists explain many cases where dig works on a laptop but the application fails.

dns-tls-pki-tls-handshake-and-certificat.r: After a certificate renewal customers could use the site, but a partner's server calls failed. The renewal had installed only the leaf file. Browsers fetched the intermediate on their own; the partner's client could not. Using the full chain fixed it.
dns-tls-pki-tls-handshake-and-certificat.x: Serve the leaf and the intermediates. Browsers hide missing intermediates, but curl, Java and mobile clients do not, so always test from outside with a strict client after every renewal.

dns-tls-pki-certificate-lifecycle-and-au.r: An internal deployment tool stopped working on a Monday morning because its certificate had expired over the weekend. It had been issued by hand years earlier and was in no inventory. All endpoints moved to automated issuance with an expiry alert.
dns-tls-pki-certificate-lifecycle-and-au.x: Automation fails quietly, so monitor from outside and alert early enough to act. Keep an inventory so forgotten internal endpoints are found before they expire, and never reuse a leaked key.

dns-tls-pki-mtls-and-internal-certificat.r: At 3 a.m. on a Sunday every service-to-service call failed with an expired certificate, even though all leaf certificates had been renewed that day. The intermediate CA had expired and nobody monitored it. A new intermediate and a two-CA bundle restored traffic.
dns-tls-pki-mtls-and-internal-certificat.x: The hard parts are distribution and rotation, not cryptography. Put CA certificates on the same expiry alerts as leaf certificates, and rotate by trusting the new CA first, then issuing, then removing the old one.

dns-tls-pki-outage-prevention-checklist.r: A company's main domain stopped resolving on a Friday evening, taking down the website, email and single sign-on. Renewal notices went to a former employee and the card on file had expired. A role-based account, auto-renew and expiry alerts followed.
dns-tls-pki-outage-prevention-checklist.x: Assign ownership to roles, not people. Registrar contacts, payment methods and DNS credentials must survive someone leaving, and recovery steps for domain or provider loss must be written down in advance.
